items.name: Paracetamol
items.how: Central COX inhibition; weak peripheral anti-inflammatory effect
hx: Peripheral COX inhibition; strong anti-inflammatory effect
It acts mainly centrally, with little anti-inflammatory effect (unlike NSAIDs).
Central μ-opioid agonism; weak peripheral effect
It isn't an opioid; it inhibits COX centrally.
Central 5-HT3 antagonism; weak peripheral anti-inflammatory effect
Its main action is central COX inhibition.
items.sewhy: At normal doses it's well tolerated; in overdose glutathione runs out and the toxic metabolite NAPQI damages the liver.

ci.c: Liver disease, alcohol dependence, weight <50 kg
ci.why: Less glutathione to detoxify NAPQI: reduce dose
x: More glutathione speeds clearance: increase the dose
Glutathione stores are low, so NAPQI builds up: reduce the dose.
Paracetamol is renally excreted: reduce the dose
It's metabolised by the liver; low glutathione lets NAPQI build up.
Alcohol blocks paracetamol absorption: increase the dose
No; less glutathione means NAPQI accumulates.
Treat with naloxone
Naloxone reverses opioids; paracetamol overdose needs acetylcysteine.
Treat with activated charcoal alone
Charcoal may help within an hour, but acetylcysteine is the antidote.
Treat with flumazenil
That's for benzodiazepines; use acetylcysteine.

items.name: NSAIDs
hx: Inhibit lipoxygenase → ↓ leukotrienes
They inhibit COX; blocking COX can actually shunt arachidonic acid towards leukotrienes.
Inhibit COX-1 and COX-2 → ↑ prostaglandins
Blocking COX lowers prostaglandin production.
Inhibit phospholipase A2 → ↓ arachidonic acid release
That's closer to a steroid effect; NSAIDs inhibit COX.
items.sewhy: Blocking prostaglandins removes stomach protection (ulcers, bleeding), constricts the afferent arteriole (AKI, salt retention, raised BP) and shifts arachidonic acid towards leukotrienes (bronchospasm); COX-2 selectivity raises thrombotic risk.

ci.c: Active or previous peptic ulcer / GI bleeding
x: COX-2 block raises gastric acid directly
COX-1 makes the protective gastric prostaglandins; losing them is the issue.
NSAIDs promote H. pylori growth
No; they strip prostaglandin protection.
NSAIDs raise gastrin release
No; COX-1 block removes protective prostaglandins.
Negative inotropy
They don't weaken the heart directly; they retain sodium and water.
Coronary vasospasm
No; sodium and water retention.
Potassium loss
They retain K⁺ if anything; the issue is Na⁺ and water.

ci.why: Block prostaglandin dilation of the afferent arteriole → ↓ GFR
x: Block prostaglandin constriction of the efferent arteriole → ↓ GFR
Prostaglandins dilate the afferent arteriole; losing that drops GFR.
Crystallise in the tubules → obstruction
No crystals; afferent vasoconstriction lowers GFR.
Raise angiotensin II at the afferent arteriole → ↑ GFR
They lower GFR by removing prostaglandin vasodilation.
Shunting to thromboxane → airway oedema
Arachidonic acid is shunted to leukotrienes.
Histamine release from mast cells → bronchospasm
Not histamine; COX block shunts to leukotrienes.
Prostaglandin excess → bronchospasm
Prostaglandins fall; leukotrienes rise.

ci.why: Premature closure of the ductus arteriosus
x: Premature opening of the foramen ovale
The risk is the ductus closing early.
Delayed closure of the ductus arteriosus
Prostaglandins keep the ductus open; NSAIDs close it early.
Fetal kidney stones
No; ductus closure (and oligohydramnios).
↓ statin efficacy
The concern is more MIs and strokes.
↑ heart block
No; ↑ MI and stroke.
↑ VTE only
The excess is arterial: MI and stroke.
↑ renal clearance of warfarin; double the dose
The risk is GI bleeding; add a PPI.
↑ hyperkalaemia; check U&E daily
Not the main concern; GI bleeding is.
↑ GI bleeding; give H. pylori eradication
Protect the stomach with a PPI.

items.name: Weak opioids
items.how: μ-opioid agonists (codeine is converted to morphine by CYP2D6; tramadol also inhibits 5-HT/NA reuptake)
hx: κ-opioid antagonists (codeine is converted to morphine by CYP3A4; tramadol also blocks NMDA)
They're μ agonists; codeine needs CYP2D6, and tramadol inhibits 5-HT/NA reuptake.
μ-opioid agonists (morphine is converted to codeine by CYP2D6; tramadol also releases dopamine)
Codeine is converted to morphine, and tramadol inhibits 5-HT/NA reuptake.
δ-opioid agonists (codeine acts unchanged; tramadol also inhibits COX)
Codeine is a prodrug (CYP2D6 → morphine); tramadol inhibits 5-HT/NA reuptake.
items.sewhy: μ-opioid effects cause constipation, nausea and drowsiness; tramadol also blocks serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake (serotonin syndrome, lowered seizure threshold).

ci.c: Children under 12, or under 18 after tonsillectomy (codeine)
ci.why: Ultra-rapid metabolisers make excess morphine → respiratory arrest
x: Poor metabolisers make no morphine → uncontrolled pain
The danger is ultra-rapid metabolisers making too much morphine.
Children can't convert codeine, so it causes seizures
Some convert it too fast, making excess morphine.
Ultra-rapid metabolisers make excess morphine → severe constipation
The dangerous effect is respiratory depression.
Codeine stops milk production
Not the reason; morphine reaches the baby.
Codeine causes neonatal jaundice
No; morphine passes to the baby (sedation, apnoea).
Codeine makes milk taste bitter
No; morphine passes into milk.
Raises antiepileptic levels
No; tramadol lowers the seizure threshold.
Blocks antiepileptic absorption
No; it lowers the seizure threshold.
Raises the seizure threshold
It lowers it.
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
That's antipsychotics; tramadol plus SSRIs causes serotonin syndrome.
Malignant hyperthermia
That comes from anaesthetic agents; tramadol plus SSRIs causes serotonin syndrome.
Respiratory depression
Not the combination's main risk; serotonin syndrome.

items.name: Strong opioids
items.how: μ-opioid receptor agonists in brain and spinal cord
hx: κ-opioid receptor antagonists in brain and spinal cord
Morphine and oxycodone are μ agonists.
μ-opioid receptor antagonists in the gut only
They're agonists acting centrally (and in the gut).
NMDA receptor antagonists in the spinal cord
That's ketamine; strong opioids are μ agonists.
items.sewhy: μ-receptors in the gut (constipation), CTZ (nausea), brainstem (respiratory depression), cortex (sedation) and bladder (retention), plus histamine release (itch); tolerance and dependence develop.

ci.c: Respiratory depression or acute type 2 respiratory failure
x: Triggers bronchospasm through histamine release
The issue is reduced respiratory drive.
Raises the brainstem's sensitivity to CO₂
They blunt the response to CO₂.
Paralyses the diaphragm directly
No; they suppress the brainstem's respiratory drive.
Speeds gut motility
Opioids slow the gut.
Causes gut ischaemia
No; they stop motility.
Raises gut secretions
They reduce secretions and motility.

ci.why: CO₂ retention raises ICP; masks pupils and GCS
x: CO₂ loss lowers ICP; dilates pupils
Opioids cause CO₂ retention (raising ICP) and pinpoint pupils.
Raises BP, increasing ICP; masks headache
The issue is CO₂ retention and masking pupils and GCS.
Causes seizures that raise ICP
Not seizures; CO₂ retention and masked neuro signs.

ci.why: Active metabolites accumulate; use oxycodone or alfentanil
x: Morphine is nephrotoxic; use codeine
Not nephrotoxic; its active metabolites build up (and codeine is worse).
Active metabolites are lost in urine; double the dose
They accumulate, so switch to oxycodone or alfentanil.
Inactive metabolites accumulate; no change needed
Morphine-6-glucuronide is active and accumulates.
Combined hypertension
The risk is combined respiratory depression.
Combined seizures
No; respiratory depression.
Combined hepatotoxicity
No; combined respiratory depression.

items.name: Naloxone
hx: Non-competitive κ-opioid agonist
It's a competitive μ antagonist.
Partial μ-opioid agonist
That's buprenorphine; naloxone is a pure antagonist.
Respiratory stimulant at the brainstem
It works by displacing opioids from μ receptors.
items.sewhy: Naloxone displaces opioids from their receptors, so a big dose triggers sudden withdrawal and a sympathetic surge (agitation, hypertension, pulmonary oedema).

x: Causes respiratory arrest: avoid completely
It reverses respiratory depression; titrate to avoid withdrawal.
Has no effect in dependence: give large doses
It works, but precipitates withdrawal; titrate small doses.
Precipitates seizures: give diazepam first
The issue is acute withdrawal; titrate.

ci.why: Naloxone wears off first → re-sedation; may need an infusion
x: Naloxone lasts longer → prolonged withdrawal; give one dose
Naloxone is shorter-acting, so sedation can return.
Long-acting opioids block naloxone completely
It works, but wears off first.
Naloxone converts to an opioid → re-sedation
No; it wears off before the opioid does.

items.name: Acetylcysteine
hx: Blocks paracetamol absorption from the gut
That's activated charcoal; acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione.
Binds paracetamol in the blood for renal excretion
It restores glutathione, which neutralises NAPQI.
Inhibits CYP2E1 so less NAPQI forms
It replenishes glutathione to mop up NAPQI.
items.sewhy: The IV infusion causes histamine release (anaphylactoid, not true allergy), with rash, flushing or bronchospasm, usually early; slowing or pausing the infusion helps.

ci.why: Higher risk of bronchospasm; still give if indicated
x: Higher risk of bronchospasm; never give
Still give it if indicated: liver failure is far worse.
Interacts with salbutamol; withhold inhalers
No; anaphylactoid bronchospasm is more likely, but still treat.
Raises theophylline levels; check levels first
Not the reason; bronchospasm risk, but still give.

items.name: Adrenaline
items.how: α1 vasoconstriction, β1 ↑ heart rate and force, β2 bronchodilation, mast-cell stabilisation
hx: α1 vasodilation, β1 ↓ heart rate and force, β2 bronchoconstriction, mast-cell activation
Each effect is reversed: it constricts vessels, speeds the heart, opens airways and stabilises mast cells.
α2 vasoconstriction only, with no cardiac or airway effects
It acts on α1, β1 and β2 receptors.
H1 receptor block, β1 ↑ heart rate, β2 bronchodilation, mast-cell stabilisation
No antihistamine action; α1 vasoconstriction is key.
items.sewhy: Stimulating α and β receptors raises heart rate and BP and can cause arrhythmias; β effects cause tremor and anxiety, and glycogenolysis raises glucose.

ci.why: May respond poorly; glucagon can help. No contraindication in anaphylaxis or arrest
x: Contraindicated: give chlorphenamine instead in anaphylaxis
Adrenaline is never contraindicated in anaphylaxis or arrest; give glucagon if the response is poor.
Response is exaggerated, so halve the dose
Response may be poor, not exaggerated; glucagon can help.
May respond poorly; give insulin to help
Glucagon (not insulin) bypasses the β receptor.

items.name: Noradrenaline
hx: Mainly β2 agonist → vasodilation, ↓ SVR
It's mainly α1: vasoconstriction raising SVR.
Mainly β1 agonist → ↑ heart rate, ↓ SVR
Its main effect is α1 vasoconstriction.
Mainly α2 agonist → ↓ sympathetic outflow, ↓ SVR
That's clonidine; noradrenaline constricts vessels through α1.
items.sewhy: Strong α1 vasoconstriction raises BP but can starve fingers, toes and gut of blood; leaking from the vein causes local necrosis.

ci.why: Constricting an empty circulation → organ ischaemia; give fluids first
x: Dilating an empty circulation → hypotension; give fluids first
It constricts vessels; in an empty circulation that starves organs.
Causes fluid overload → pulmonary oedema; give diuretics first
The circulation is empty; fill it before constricting.
Raises heart rate → arrhythmias; give beta-blockers first
The issue is constricting an empty circulation; give fluids first.

items.name: Atropine
hx: Muscarinic agonist → increases vagal slowing
It blocks muscarinic receptors, removing vagal tone.
β1 agonist → directly speeds the SA node
It works by blocking vagal (muscarinic) input.
Nicotinic antagonist → blocks sympathetic ganglia
It's antimuscarinic.
items.sewhy: Blocking muscarinic receptors removes parasympathetic tone: tachycardia, dry mouth, urinary retention, blurred vision and, in older people, confusion.

ci.why: Antimuscarinic effects; in emergencies benefit usually outweighs this
x: Cholinergic effects; never use in emergencies
It's antimuscarinic, and in emergencies the benefit usually wins.
α-adrenergic effects; use half-dose in emergencies
The issue is antimuscarinic effects; benefit usually outweighs risk.
Antimuscarinic effects; always contraindicated, even in emergencies
In emergencies the benefit usually outweighs this.

items.name: Entonox
hx: Inhaled anaesthetic vapour
It's a 50:50 N₂O/O₂ analgesic gas, not a volatile anaesthetic.
Inhaled bronchodilator gas
It's an analgesic.
Inhaled opioid aerosol
It's nitrous oxide and oxygen.
se: B12 inactivation with prolonged or recreational use
items.sewhy: Nitrous oxide causes nausea and dizziness; it oxidises the cobalt in B12, so prolonged or recreational use causes deficiency and neuropathy.

ci.why: N₂O diffuses into air spaces and expands them
x: N₂O constricts the pleura and traps air
N₂O enters gas spaces faster than nitrogen leaves, expanding them.
Oxygen dissolves the air, shrinking it too fast
No; N₂O expands air spaces.
N₂O causes bronchospasm
No; it expands air-filled spaces.
Stops bowel peristalsis
The issue is gas expansion.
Causes bowel ischaemia directly
No; N₂O expands gas in the bowel.
Speeds bowel peristalsis
No; it expands bowel gas.

ci.why: Can raise ICP and confuse assessment
x: Can lower ICP and mask fractures
It can raise ICP and cloud the neuro assessment.
Can cause seizures in any head injury
Not the reason; raised ICP and a confused assessment.
Can cause hypoxia from bronchospasm
No; it can raise ICP and confuse assessment.
